items.title: 3.4 Solution of Equations Reducible to the Quadratic Equation

blocks.text: There are certain types of equations which do not look like equations of degree 2, but they can be reduced to a quadratic equation. We shall discuss the solutions of rational, radical and exponential equations.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The book's sentence names three kinds of equations, but this unit works out only two of them: rational equations (3.4.1) and radical equations (3.4.2). No exponential equation is solved in this unit or in Exercise 3.2, so you need only the two methods below.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
First recall what we are reducing to. A quadratic equation is an equation of degree 2 that can be written in the standard form
\[ax^{2} + bx + c = 0,\quad a \ne 0\]
It can be solved by factorisation, by completing the square, or by the quadratic formula below. "Reducible to a quadratic" means: the equation is not in this form at first (there is a variable in a denominator, under a square root, or a higher power), but a few legal steps turn it into this form.

blocks.text_alt: x equals minus b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4 a c, all over 2 a

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The general plan for every equation in 3.4:
1. Write down the restrictions first: a denominator must not be zero, and an expression under a square root must not be negative.
2. Remove the "difficult" part: multiply by the common denominator (rational equations), or isolate a radical and square (radical equations).
3. Simplify and bring every term to one side, so that you get \(ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\).
4. Solve the quadratic.
5. Check every value you found in the ORIGINAL equation and reject any value that breaks a restriction or does not satisfy it.
Step 5 is not optional: the steps of the method can create values that are not real solutions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our own illustration of "reducible" (not from the book): \(x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4 = 0\) has degree 4, but it is a quadratic in \(x^{2}\). Put \(y = x^{2}\):
\[y^{2} - 5y + 4 = 0\]
\[(y - 1)(y - 4) = 0\]
\[y = 1 \ \text{or}\ y = 4\]
Going back to \(x\): \(x^{2} = 1\) gives \(x = \pm 1\), and \(x^{2} = 4\) gives \(x = \pm 2\). So the solution set is \(\{-2, -1, 1, 2\}\). The idea is always the same: change the look of the equation until a quadratic appears.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Some equations are not quadratic at first sight but become quadratic after a few legal steps.
2. Rational equations: clear the denominators with the LCD (3.4.1).
3. Radical equations: isolate a radical and square (3.4.2).
4. Always write the restrictions first and check every answer in the original equation.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Stopping at the quadratic's roots without checking them in the original equation.
2. Forgetting the restrictions: a value that makes a denominator zero, or a square root of a negative number, is never a solution.
3. Solving the substituted quadratic (for example in \(y = x^{2}\)) and forgetting to go back to \(x\).
